title: Dragonfly
summary: Dragonfly, also tracked as Energetic Bear and Berserk Bear, is a Russian state-linked activity set that public reporting associates with espionage and pre-positioning against energy, utility, nuclear, aviation and defence organisations, and more recently information technology and service providers. Early campaigns used strategic web compromise and malicious installers disguised as industrial control software from legitimate vendors, letting operators reach engineering workstations. Reporting later described a shift toward credential theft and remote access through virtual private network services, including abuse of multi-factor authentication enrolment weaknesses, followed by movement into operational technology environments. The two-track behaviour matters, because some activity looks like collection and other activity looks like preparation for disruption.

beginner.definition: Dragonfly is a name for attacks that public reports link to Russian state interests. It targets energy companies, utilities and their suppliers. Early campaigns used fake software updates for industrial equipment. Later activity focused on stealing credentials and entering through remote access services.
beginner.whyItMatters: Energy and utility companies keep everyday life running, so they attract attention from state groups. Attackers often reach them through a smaller supplier instead of attacking directly. That means your security also depends on the companies you work with. Watching logins and remote access closely is one of the strongest defences here. Ignoring either one leaves a door open.
howItWorks: The attackers identify energy companies and the smaller suppliers and service providers they depend on.
They use fake software installers, phishing or stolen credentials to get an account inside.
They log in through remote access services, which can look like normal staff working from home.
They enrol their own authentication device, so the stolen password keeps working.
From there they reach engineering systems and study how equipment is controlled.
They stay in place, collecting information and quietly preparing for possible later action.
beginner.example: Think of a stadium where the main gates are well guarded. The catering vans, however, are waved through with a quick glance. Someone hides in a van, then walks into the control room where the lights and doors are managed. The strongest gate is useless if a side route is left open.
takeaways: Your security depends on your suppliers, so third-party access deserves the same checks as your own.
Watch for new authentication devices being added, because that keeps a stolen password useful.
Stolen credentials plus remote access is one of the most common ways into critical networks.

objectives: Describe Dragonfly and the sectors its documented campaigns target.
Explain how a compromised supplier becomes a route into a larger, better-defended organisation.
Explain why enrolling a new authentication device preserves an attacker's access.
Identify the authentication and network evidence that reveals this activity.
Distinguish espionage activity from pre-positioning and explain why the difference matters.
Present the group's public attribution with source and stated confidence.
